props.title: McQ

sections.content: McQ represents John Wayne's fascinating late-career pivot into contemporary crime thrillers, following the massive success of Dirty Harry (1971). Wayne plays Lt. Lon McQ, a Seattle detective investigating police corruption and drug trafficking in a grittier, more urban setting than his iconic Westerns. The film deliberately echoes elements of Bullitt (1968) and The French Connection (1971), particularly in its muscular car chases through Seattle's industrial districts. Director John Sturges, who previously worked with Wayne on The Magnificent Seven (1960), brings his trademark action expertise while wrestling with the Duke's aging screen presence.

sections.content: The 1970s marked a dramatic shift in police thrillers, moving from black-and-white morality to complex examinations of corruption and institutional failure. Serpico (1973) and The New Centurions (1972) portrayed cops struggling with systemic corruption, while The Seven-Ups (1973) doubled down on gritty realism. McQ fits somewhat uncomfortably in this new landscape, with Wayne's traditional heroic persona clashing against the era's growing cynicism.

The film's technical achievements deserve recognition, particularly the innovative use of the MAC-10 submachine gun (its first appearance in cinema) and the spectacular beach car chase using actual Pontiac Trans Ams. These elements influenced later police actioners like Mitchell (1975) and Magnum Force (1973), though McQ's more traditional approach feels like a bridge between classic Hollywood and the emerging crime thriller style. sections.content: Wayne's attempt to modernize his image through McQ parallels similar efforts by aging stars like Robert Mitchum in The Friends of Eddie Coyle (1973) and Kirk Douglas in The Detective (1968). These films marked a transition period where Old Hollywood titans grappled with the new reality of morally ambiguous law enforcement narratives that would eventually lead to films like To Live and Die in L.A. (1985).
